analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal oversight of large non-bank financial companies under the Dodd-Frank law.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in August 2012 to roll back Dodd-Frank's oversight of large non-bank financial companies, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 financial crisis, the Dodd-Frank law let regulators designate big non-bank financial firms — insurers, asset managers, and others outside traditional banking — for stricter Federal Reserve supervision. This bill would repeal that authority entirely: no more designation of systemically important non-bank firms, no heightened capital or leverage standards for them, no mandatory resolution plans, and it would also repeal the law's supervision of payment and clearing systems. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large non-bank financial companies — the insurers, diversified financial firms, and asset managers that could be designated for stricter Federal Reserve supervision — would be freed from heightened capital, leverage, and resolution-planning requirements, along with the cost of reporting and examinations. Their shareholders and executives gain from lighter oversight.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the Federal Reserve's authority to supervise nonbank financial companies designated as systemically important, along with the heightened prudential standards, leverage requirements, and reporting duties that come with that designation.

It eliminates the Financial Stability Oversight Council's power to designate systemically important firms and market utilities, repeals the Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision Act, and ends requirements for resolution plans, credit exposure reports, and related studies.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, in the form of a higher chance that a large non-bank firm's failure spreads through the financial system and again requires taxpayer-supported rescues, as with AIG in 2008 — the scenario Dodd-Frank's nonbank oversight was written to prevent.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Dodd-Frank's authority over nonbank financial companies would have stripped regulators of the power to identify, examine, and impose heightened standards on large financial firms outside the banking system — the category that included AIG — increasing the risk that a failure at one of them again requires taxpayer-supported rescues.
It would also have repealed supervision of financial market utilities and payment, clearing, and settlement systems, removing oversight of the plumbing that payments and markets run on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's burden fell on a tool Congress built after the 2008 crisis precisely to catch non-bank giants like AIG before they could take down the system; removing it saved those firms compliance costs while restoring the gap that let the crisis spread. It never became law, so no such cost was imposed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in August 2012 and died there when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013, with no cosponsors and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Vitter introduced the bill on August 2, 2012, near the end of the 112th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action was taken before Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large nonbank financial companies avoided having the Dodd-Frank oversight regime rolled back, but they also faced no near-term threat of the bill passing; the 2010 law's provisions remained on the books unchanged.

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Dodd-Frank's nonbank financial company oversight provisions.

sides.party_line_note: Only the Republican sponsor is on the record; no votes occurred and no other senator took a position in the record.

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies (diversified financial firms, insurers, asset managers)
industries.note: The bill removes the threat of Fed designation, which carries stricter capital, leverage, and resolution-planning requirements, freeing these firms from the most demanding layer of post-crisis regulation.

Repealing Title VIII of Dodd-Frank ends dedicated federal risk-management supervision of these market plumbing firms, removing a compliance burden but also a source of stability for the payments system everyone relies on.
